t.6.26.2: Then, having heard that roar, Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, sank into thought for a moment and looked up at his ministers.
t.6.26.1: To the sound of kettledrums mingled with the blare of conches, the mighty-armed Rāghava, Rāma, conqueror of enemy cities, advanced.
t.6.26.3: Then the mighty Rāvaṇa, having addressed all those ministers there, spoke thus, making the whole assembly resound.
t.6.26.4: What you have said about Rāma, his crossing of the ocean, his valour and the mass of his forces, all that I have heard; and I also know you yourselves to be of true prowess in battle.
t.6.26.5: Then, having heard Rāvaṇa's words, the exceedingly wise rākṣasa named Mālyavant, his grandfather on his mother's side, spoke.
t.6.26.6: O king, the ruler who is well trained in the branches of knowledge and who follows sound policy exercises sovereignty for a long time and brings his enemies under his control.
t.6.26.8: A king who is declining in strength, or one who is equal in power, should make peace. One should not despise an enemy; only one who is superior should wage war.
t.6.26.7: Indeed, one who makes peace with his enemies and wages war against them as the time demands, and who strengthens his own side, attains great sovereignty.
t.6.26.10: All the divine sages and the gandharvas desire his victory. Do not enter into hostility with him; let peace with him be pleasing to you.
t.6.26.9: This is what pleases me, O Rāvaṇa: peace with Rāma. Let Sītā, on whose account we have been attacked, be given back to him.
t.6.26.11: The blessed Grandsire created just two factions, that of the suras and that of the asuras, and with them dharma and adharma as the foundations on which each of them rests.
t.6.26.12: Dharma, it is said, is the side of the gods and of the great-souled ones; adharma, O Rāvaṇa, is the side of the rākṣasas and the asuras.
t.6.26.13: When righteousness devours unrighteousness, the Kṛta age comes into being; when unrighteousness devours righteousness, the Tiṣya age sets in.
t.6.26.14: Therefore, as you roamed the worlds, great righteousness was struck down by you and unrighteousness was embraced; because of that, our enemies are stronger than we are.
t.6.26.15: That adharma of yours, grown great through your heedlessness, is a serpent that is devouring us, while the one who sustains the gods strengthens the side of the gods.
t.6.26.16: By you, attached to sensual pleasures and acting just as you please, great distress has been caused to the sages, who are like fire. Their power is irresistible, like a blazing fire.
t.6.26.17: These twice-born men, their souls purified by austerity and devoted to upholding dharma, constantly worship with all those various principal sacrifices.
t.6.26.19: The smoke rising from the agnihotra fires of the fire-like sages, pervading the ten directions, takes away the splendour of the rākṣasas.
t.6.26.18: They duly offer oblations into the sacred fires and loudly recite the Vedas; overpowering the Rākṣasas, they raised the sounds of Vedic chanting, and all have fled scattering in every direction, like a thundercloud in the hot season.
t.6.26.20: In those various holy regions, the fierce austerity being practised by those firm in their vows sorely torments the Rākṣasas.
t.6.26.21: Having seen portents of various kinds, dreadful and manifold, I foresee the destruction of all the rākṣasas.
t.6.26.22: Dreadful, terrifying clouds, thundering harshly, rain down warm blood upon Laṅkā on every side.
t.6.26.23: Teardrops fall from the weeping mounts, and the banners, battered and discolored, do not shine as they did before.
t.6.26.24: Beasts of prey, jackals and vultures howl and shriek most dreadfully, and, entering Laṅkā, they ceaselessly gather together in packs.
t.6.26.25: Dark women, standing before us, laugh with their pale teeth; in dreams they speak back in reply and plunder our houses.
t.6.26.26: Dogs devour the bali offerings of the households; donkeys are born from cows, and rats mingle together with mongooses.
t.6.26.28: Pale birds with red feet, and doves too, impelled by Time, are roaming about for the destruction of the Rākṣasas.
t.6.26.27: Cats came together with leopards, boars with dogs, and Kiṃnaras with Rākṣasas and with humans as well.
t.6.26.29: The mynas kept in the houses, screeching "cīcīkūcī," fall down locked together, and those eager for a fight are vanquished.
t.6.26.31: We consider Rāma to be Viṣṇu, who has taken on a human body; for that Rāghava of firm valour is surely no mere man.
t.6.26.30: A frightful, misshapen, shaven-headed man, black, of a dark and tawny hue, peers into the houses of all from time to time. These and other evil portents are arising.
t.6.26.32: O Rāvaṇa, make peace with Rāma, the king of men, by whom that most wondrous bridge across the ocean was built.
t.6.26.33: Having spoken these words there, the mighty Mālyavān, supreme in valour even among the unsurpassed, once more searched the mind of the lord of the rākṣasas and, gazing at Rāvaṇa, fell silent.
